main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced theories and principles of Fine Art
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of forms of Fine Art in East and West Africa
learning_activity_name: Analyse forms of Fine Art in East and West African societies
sla_name: Forms of Fine Art in East and West African societies
sla_assessment_criteria: Forms of Fine Art (drawing, paintings and prints) in East and West African societies are well analysed.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: East and West African societies have produced distinct forms of Fine Art, including drawing, painting and printmaking, each carrying its own tools, materials and social functions.
sla_notes_details: In East Africa, forms of Fine Art include rock and cave paintings (such as those found at Kondoa in Tanzania), bark-cloth decoration, and contemporary Tingatinga painting characterised by bright flat colours and stylised animal subjects. In West Africa, notable forms include Adinkra and Adire cloth printing from Ghana and Nigeria, Benin bronze relief work, and Nsibidi ideographic drawing. Across both regions, Fine Art traditionally served social functions such as recording history, marking status, religious ritual and storytelling, using locally available materials like natural pigments, clay, bark and dyes rather than imported manufactured materials. Comparing the two regions shows shared uses of pattern and symbolism but different subject matter and technique shaped by local culture and available resources.
sla_notes_illustrations: A Tingatinga painting of a lion in flat, bright colours from Tanzania can be compared with an Adinkra cloth print from Ghana bearing symbolic geometric patterns, showing two different East and West African approaches to Fine Art that both communicate cultural meaning.
sla_notes_daily_life: Students can find these forms of Fine Art in local curio shops, cultural centres and printed kanga or kitenge fabric designs that are part of everyday Tanzanian life.
sla_exercise: Name one form of Fine Art found in East Africa and one found in West Africa.::East Africa: Tingatinga painting or rock art (e.g. Kondoa); West Africa: Adinkra/Adire cloth printing or Benin bronze relief.||State one social function of Fine Art in traditional African societies.::Recording history, marking social status, or supporting religious ritual and storytelling (any one).||What materials were traditionally used to create Fine Art in East and West Africa before manufactured materials became available?::Locally available materials such as natural pigments, clay, bark and plant dyes.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced theories and principles of Fine Art
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of basic principles of curating works of Fine Art
learning_activity_name: Describe the basic principles of curating drawings, paintings and prints
sla_name: Basic principles of curating drawings, paintings and prints
sla_assessment_criteria: The basic principles of curating drawings, paintings and prints are well described.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Curating is the process of selecting, organising, preserving and presenting artworks so that they can be understood, protected and appreciated by an audience.
sla_notes_details: Basic principles of curating drawings, paintings and prints include selection (choosing works that fit a theme, quality standard or historical significance), documentation (recording the artist, title, date, medium and condition of each work), proper handling and storage (using acid-free materials, controlling humidity and light to prevent fading or damage), thoughtful display (arranging works by theme, chronology or visual relationship so viewers can follow a narrative), and interpretation (providing labels or information that help the audience understand the work's meaning and context). A curator balances artistic value with the practical needs of preservation and public access.
sla_notes_illustrations: A school planning an art exhibition would first select the best drawings and paintings from students, label each with the artist's name and title, arrange them by theme around the hall, and protect fragile paper works from direct sunlight.
sla_notes_daily_life: Art galleries, museums and even a family arranging photographs and drawings at home for display all apply these same basic curating principles of selection, care and presentation.
sla_exercise: Define curating as it applies to Fine Art.::The process of selecting, organising, preserving and presenting artworks for an audience.||State one principle of proper handling and storage of drawings and paintings.::Using acid-free materials and controlling light and humidity to prevent fading or damage.||Why is documentation an important part of curating an artwork?::It records details such as artist, title, date and medium, which helps preserve the artwork's history and value.

learning_activity_name: Create single object still images using drawing and painting methods
sla_name: Creating single object still images using drawing and painting methods
sla_assessment_criteria: Single object still images using drawing and painting methods are well created.
sla_teaching_aids: Manila paper|Canvas|Pencils|Paints (Water colors|Acrylic|Oil colours|Painting brushes|Palette|Linseed oil|Water|Painting|Containers|Metal peg bar|Ruler|Compass|Stapler|Glue|Push pins|Sketch book|Transparent sheets
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A still image of a single object is a foundational drawing and painting exercise that trains accurate observation of form, proportion, light and shadow.
sla_notes_details: Creating a single object still image begins with careful observation of the object's shape, proportion and the direction of light falling on it, followed by a light pencil outline establishing basic proportions, then building up form using shading techniques (hatching, cross-hatching, blending) for drawing, or building up layers of colour from light to dark for painting. Attention to highlights, mid-tones and shadows gives the object a three-dimensional appearance on a flat surface. Common tools include pencils, manila paper, and paints such as watercolour, acrylic or oil applied with brushes.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student drawing a single clay pot as a still object would first sketch its outline lightly, then shade the side away from the light source darker and leave the side facing the light source almost white to create the illusion of a rounded, three-dimensional pot.
sla_notes_daily_life: This same skill of observing an object's shape and shading is used when a sign-writer or product illustrator draws everyday items such as tools, fruits or household objects for advertising or instructional materials.
sla_exercise: What is the first step in creating a single object still image?::Careful observation of the object's shape, proportion and the direction of light falling on it.||Name two shading techniques used to give a drawn object a three-dimensional appearance.::Hatching and cross-hatching (or blending).||Why are highlights and shadows important when drawing a single object?::They create the illusion of three-dimensional form and light on a flat surface.

sla_assessment_criteria: Thematic composition of still images using drawing and painting methods are well created.

sla_notes_intro: A thematic composition arranges several still objects or images together to communicate a single unifying idea or message, going beyond a single-object study.
sla_notes_details: Creating a thematic composition begins with choosing a clear theme (for example, 'harvest' or 'market day'), selecting objects or elements that relate to that theme, and arranging them using composition principles such as balance, focal point, rule of thirds and use of foreground and background to lead the viewer's eye. The artist then applies drawing and painting methods, sketching the overall arrangement first before adding detail, tone and colour to each element so that the whole composition reads as one coherent picture rather than separate unrelated objects.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student composing a 'market day' theme might arrange a basket of fruit, a scale and a vendor's stool together in one drawing, placing the basket as the focal point in the foreground with the stool and background figures placed further back to create depth.
sla_notes_daily_life: Shop signage, calendar illustrations and packaging designs commonly use thematic compositions to communicate an idea at a glance, just as students practise in this competence.
sla_exercise: What is a thematic composition in Fine Art?::An arrangement of several objects or images that together communicate a single unifying idea or theme.||Name one composition principle used when arranging a thematic composition.::Balance (or focal point, or rule of thirds).||Why should elements in a thematic composition relate to a chosen theme?::So that the whole composition communicates one coherent idea rather than appearing as unrelated objects.

specific_competence_name: Create artistic works using various techniques
sla_assessment_criteria: Prints of various motifs are well created.
sla_teaching_aids: Screen|Mesh|Printing colours|Squeegee|Painting brushes|Photo-emulsion|Sensitizer|Paste|Water|White papers|Dish|A piece of transparent glass|Frame for screen mesh|Cloth materials|Wood glue|Office glue|Shoe tacks|Hammer|Masking tapes|Pencils|Black ink/pen|Computer|Printer
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Printmaking allows an image or motif to be reproduced multiple times from a single prepared surface, and is widely used for decorative and commercial purposes.
sla_notes_details: Creating prints of various motifs involves first designing a motif (a repeated decorative shape or pattern, such as a geometric, floral or symbolic design), then transferring it onto a printing surface such as a screen (for screen printing) using photo-emulsion and sensitiser, or a carved block or stencil for other printmaking techniques. Ink or paint is applied and pressed or squeegeed through the screen or stencil onto paper or cloth, and the process is repeated to produce multiple identical copies. Care must be taken with registration (aligning the design correctly each time) and even pressure to avoid smudging.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student designing an Adinkra-style motif of a repeated symbol can prepare a simple stencil, apply ink evenly with a squeegee, and press it onto several pieces of cloth to produce a series of identical printed motifs.
sla_notes_daily_life: Printed kitenge and kanga fabrics, T-shirt designs, and packaging labels sold in local markets are everyday examples of motifs created through printmaking techniques similar to those practised in this competence.
sla_exercise: What is a motif in printmaking?::A repeated decorative shape or pattern, such as a geometric, floral or symbolic design.||Name one material used in screen printing to transfer a motif onto the screen.::Photo-emulsion and sensitiser.||Why is registration important when printing multiple copies of a motif?::It ensures the design is aligned correctly each time so the printed copies look neat and consistent.

specific_competence_name: Create artistic works using various techniques
sla_assessment_criteria: Detailed relief realistic sculptures are well created.
sla_teaching_aids: Chisels|Carving knives|Mallets|Over-coat|Various species of wood|Soapstone|Clay|Plaster|Papier mache|Metals|Various sizes of sand-papers|Vanish|Adze
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Relief sculpture is a form of three-dimensional art in which shapes are carved or built so that they project from a flat background rather than standing fully free.
sla_notes_details: Creating a detailed realistic relief sculpture involves selecting suitable material (wood, soapstone, clay, plaster or papier mache), planning the design so its subject appears to emerge naturally from the flat background, and using tools such as chisels, carving knives and mallets to remove or add material gradually, working from rough shape to fine, realistic detail such as texture, muscle definition or facial features. Sand-papers of various grades are used to smooth the surface, and a varnish or coat may be applied to protect and finish the sculpture. Safety when handling sharp carving tools is essential throughout the process.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student carving a relief sculpture of a village scene on a wooden panel would first rough out the basic shapes of huts and figures with a mallet and chisel, then refine details such as thatched roof texture and clothing folds before sanding and varnishing the finished panel.
sla_notes_daily_life: Wood and stone relief carvings sold as souvenirs and decorative wall panels in Tanzanian curio markets are everyday examples of the detailed realistic relief sculpture skills covered in this competence.
sla_exercise: What distinguishes a relief sculpture from a fully free-standing sculpture?::A relief sculpture projects from a flat background rather than standing completely free on all sides.||Name two tools used to carve a detailed realistic relief sculpture.::Chisels and carving knives (or mallets).||Why is sanding an important step in finishing a relief sculpture?::It smooths the surface and removes rough marks left by carving, giving the sculpture a refined, realistic finish.

specific_competence_name: Create real and abstract drawings and paintings
sla_assessment_criteria: Various sketches from observation are well created.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Sketching from observation trains the artist to record what is actually seen in front of them, rather than from memory or imagination.
sla_notes_details: Creating sketches from observation involves selecting a real scene, object or person, studying its proportions, angles and light before drawing, and using quick, loose lines to capture the overall form before refining detail if time allows. Techniques include gesture sketching (capturing movement and pose quickly), contour drawing (following the outline of a subject closely) and value sketching (indicating light and shadow with tone). Repeated practice from observation sharpens hand-eye coordination and the ability to judge proportion accurately.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student observing a seated classmate might first make a quick gesture sketch capturing the overall pose and proportions within a few minutes, then spend longer refining the facial features and clothing folds while still looking directly at the model.
sla_notes_daily_life: News illustrators, court sketch artists and fashion designers all use sketching from observation to quickly and accurately capture real scenes or people for their work.
sla_exercise: What is sketching from observation?::Drawing a real scene, object or person directly as it is seen, rather than from memory or imagination.||Name one sketching technique used when observing a subject.::Gesture sketching (or contour drawing, or value sketching).||Why is sketching from observation useful practice for an artist?::It sharpens hand-eye coordination and the ability to judge proportion, light and shadow accurately.

specific_competence_name: Create real and abstract drawings and paintings
learning_activity_name: Compose sceneries from observation by drawing and painting
sla_name: Composing sceneries from observation by drawing and painting
sla_assessment_criteria: The paintings and drawing are well composed.
sla_teaching_aids: Manila paper|Canvas|Pencils|Paints|(poster|Water colours acrylic|Oil colours|Painting brushes|Palettes|Linseed oil|Water|Containers
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Composing a scenery from observation extends single-object sketching into representing a whole landscape or environment as it actually appears.
sla_notes_details: Composing a scenery from observation involves choosing a real outdoor or indoor view, establishing the horizon line and overall composition first, then working from background to foreground (distant elements such as sky and hills painted first, closer elements such as trees or buildings added afterward) to create a sense of depth (aerial perspective, where distant objects appear lighter and less detailed). Drawing and painting methods, including linear perspective for buildings and roads, and colour mixing to match observed light conditions, are combined to produce a believable representation of the scene.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student painting a view of a village from a hilltop would paint the distant hills in pale, soft blue tones first, then add darker, more detailed trees and houses in the foreground to create a convincing sense of distance.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local landscape and cityscape paintings sold by street artists, and photographs used for tourism promotion, both rely on the same principles of depth and perspective that students practise when composing sceneries from observation.
sla_exercise: What should an artist establish first when composing a scenery from observation?::The horizon line and the overall composition of the scene.||Explain aerial perspective in landscape painting.::A technique where distant objects are painted lighter in colour and less detailed to create a sense of depth.||In what order should elements of a scenery normally be painted to create depth?::From background to foreground, distant elements first and closer elements added afterward.

specific_competence_name: Use ICT to design and create works of Fine Art
learning_activity_name: Use computer software to create drawings, paintings and prints
sla_name: Using computer software to create drawings, paintings and prints
sla_assessment_criteria: Drawings, paintings and prints are well created.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Digital art tools now allow artists to create drawings, paintings and prints on a computer, offering new techniques alongside traditional hand methods.
sla_notes_details: Using computer software for Fine Art involves selecting an appropriate programme for the task, drawing or painting digitally using a mouse, stylus or touchscreen, working with layers to separate and edit different parts of an image without affecting the rest, applying digital brushes, colour fills and filters to achieve different effects, and exporting or printing the finished digital artwork. Compared with traditional methods, digital software allows easy correction of mistakes, unlimited colour experimentation, and quick production of multiple print-ready versions of a design.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student designing a poster digitally can sketch the layout on one layer, add colour on a separate layer beneath it, and adjust the colours repeatedly without damaging the original sketch, something that is far more difficult with traditional paint on paper.
sla_notes_daily_life: Many local sign-writers, T-shirt printers and graphic designers in Tanzania now design their artwork digitally before printing, showing how this competence connects directly to real creative businesses.
sla_exercise: Name one advantage of using computer software over traditional methods to create art.::Mistakes can be corrected easily and colours experimented with freely without damaging the original work.||What is the purpose of using layers in digital art software?::To separate different parts of an image so each can be edited independently without affecting the rest.||Give one example of computer software or tool used to create digital drawings and paintings.::A drawing/painting programme used with a mouse, stylus or touchscreen (for example an image-editing application).

specific_competence_name: Prepare a portfolio of Fine Art works
learning_activity_name: Create a portfolio of the best artworks created during the year
sla_name: Preparing a portfolio of the best Fine Art works created during the year
sla_assessment_criteria: The completed portfolio of Fine Art work are well created.
sla_teaching_aids: Art works|Memory card|Computer|Manila sheet|Stapling machine|Tapes|Scissors|Paper cutting machine|Vinyl|Fabric materials
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A portfolio is a curated collection of an artist's best work, assembled to demonstrate skill, range and development over a period of time.
sla_notes_details: Preparing a Fine Art portfolio involves reviewing all the artworks created during the year, selecting only the strongest and most varied pieces that show a range of techniques (drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture), organising the selected works in a logical order (for example by technique or by date of creation), and presenting them neatly, mounted or protected in a folder, sleeve or bound book, often with a short label or caption for each piece. A well-prepared portfolio should tell a clear story of the artist's growing skill and should be free of damaged, unfinished or repetitive work.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student assembling a portfolio for assessment might choose one strong drawing, one painting and one print from the year's work, mount each neatly on manila sheets, and arrange them in the order the skills were learned, with the most advanced piece placed last.
sla_notes_daily_life: Job seekers in creative fields such as graphic design, tailoring and photography commonly prepare similar portfolios to showcase their best work to potential employers or clients.
sla_exercise: What is a Fine Art portfolio?::A curated collection of an artist's best and most varied work, assembled to show skill and development.||State one criterion for selecting work to include in a portfolio.::Choosing the strongest, most varied pieces that show a range of techniques (and avoiding damaged or repetitive work).||Why should a portfolio be presented neatly and in a logical order?::So that it clearly and professionally communicates the artist's skill and progress to anyone viewing it.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced theories and principles of Fine Art
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of forms of Fine Art in East and West Africa
learning_activity_name: Analyse forms of sculpture and animation in East and West African societies
sla_name: Forms of sculpture and animation in East and West African societies
sla_assessment_criteria: Forms of sculpture and animation in East and West African societies are well analysed.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Beyond drawing, painting and prints, East and West African societies also developed distinct traditions of sculpture and, more recently, animation.
sla_notes_details: In East Africa, sculpture forms include Makonde ebony carving from Tanzania and Mozambique, noted for elongated, intertwined human figures, and traditional wood stools and masks used in ceremonies. In West Africa, sculpture forms include Benin bronze and ivory court sculpture, Yoruba wood carving, and Akan gold-weight figures, often linked to kingship, ancestor veneration and spiritual belief. Animation is a newer form of Fine Art in both regions, growing from traditional storytelling and increasingly produced using digital tools by young African animators who adapt folktales and contemporary stories into moving images, often reflecting the same symbolism and social themes found in traditional sculpture.
sla_notes_illustrations: A Makonde ebony sculpture of intertwined human figures from Tanzania can be compared with a Yoruba wooden mask from West Africa to show two distinct sculptural traditions, while a short animated folktale produced by a young Tanzanian animator shows how these older forms inspire new digital Fine Art.
sla_notes_daily_life: Makonde carvings sold in local curio markets and animated cartoons shared on social media by young Tanzanian creators are both examples students can find in their own communities.
sla_exercise: Name one sculptural tradition from East Africa and one from West Africa.::East Africa: Makonde ebony carving; West Africa: Benin bronze sculpture or Yoruba wood carving.||What social or spiritual role did much traditional African sculpture serve?::It was linked to kingship, ancestor veneration, ceremony or spiritual belief.||How does modern African animation relate to traditional Fine Art forms?::It often adapts traditional storytelling and symbolism from sculpture and folktales into moving digital images.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of some advanced theories and principles of Fine Art
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of basic principles of curating works of Fine Art
learning_activity_name: Describe the basic principles of curating sculpture and animation artworks
sla_name: Basic principles of curating sculpture and animation artworks
sla_assessment_criteria: The basic principles of curating sculptures and animations are well described.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Curating sculpture and animation requires principles adapted from general art curating but suited to three-dimensional objects and moving digital images.
sla_notes_details: For sculpture, curating principles include careful handling and secure display stands to prevent damage or toppling, controlling environmental conditions such as humidity to prevent cracking of wood or clay, and documenting the material, technique and cultural meaning of each piece. For animation, curating principles include preserving digital files in accessible formats and with backups, organising a viewing programme or screening order that suits the audience and time available, and providing context, such as the theme or technique used, so viewers understand each piece. In both cases, the curator's role is to protect the artwork's physical or digital integrity while presenting it meaningfully to an audience.
sla_notes_illustrations: A school preparing an exhibition might place wooden sculptures on stable stands away from direct sunlight and humidity, while displaying short student animations on a screen in a planned order with brief spoken introductions explaining each one's theme.
sla_notes_daily_life: Museums that display carved artefacts and film festivals that screen animated shorts both apply these same curating principles suited to solid objects and moving images respectively.
sla_exercise: Name one curating consideration specific to sculpture.::Secure, stable display stands and control of humidity to prevent damage (cracking, toppling).||Name one curating consideration specific to animation.::Preserving digital files in accessible formats with backups, and organising a suitable screening order.||What is the curator's overall role for both sculpture and animation?::To protect the artwork's integrity while presenting it meaningfully to an audience.

learning_activity_name: Create and animate illustrations using computer software
sla_name: Creating and animating illustrations using computer software
sla_assessment_criteria: Illustrations using computer software are well created and animated.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Animation brings still illustrations to life by creating an illusion of movement through a sequence of images displayed quickly one after another.
sla_notes_details: Creating and animating illustrations using computer software (such as Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, After Effects or GIMP) begins with designing individual illustrations or characters, then creating a sequence of slightly changed frames or using software tools such as keyframes and tweening, where the software automatically generates the frames between a starting and ending position, to produce smooth movement. Timing (how long each frame is shown) controls the speed and realism of the motion. The finished animation is exported as a video file that can be shared or used within a larger production.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student animating a simple bouncing ball would set a keyframe showing the ball at the top of its bounce and another keyframe showing it at the bottom, letting the software automatically generate the in-between frames to create smooth, realistic movement.
sla_notes_daily_life: Animated advertisements, cartoon programmes and social media stickers that Tanzanian youth watch and share daily are produced using the same computer animation principles taught in this competence.
sla_exercise: What is tweening in computer animation?::A software process that automatically generates the in-between frames between a starting and ending keyframe to create smooth movement.||Name one software programme used for creating and animating illustrations.::Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, After Effects or GIMP (any one).||Why does the timing of frames matter in animation?::It controls the speed and realism of the movement shown to the viewer.

specific_competence_name: Create artistic works using various techniques
learning_activity_name: Print patterns of themes for specific purposes
sla_name: Printing patterns of themes for specific purposes
sla_assessment_criteria: Patterns with themes for specific purpose are well printed.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Printed patterns are often designed for a defined practical or commercial purpose, such as fabric for a specific event, packaging, or promotional material.
sla_notes_details: Printing patterns of themes for specific purposes involves first identifying the purpose and audience (for example a pattern for a wedding kitenge, a school uniform fabric, or a product label), designing a motif or pattern that reflects the chosen theme, preparing the printing surface (screen, stencil or block) accordingly, and testing the print on a sample material before producing the full run to check colour, scale and registration are correct for the intended use. Consideration of the final material (cloth, paper, or another surface) affects choice of ink and printing technique.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student designing a pattern for a school anniversary T-shirt would create a motif using the school's colours and emblem, test print it on a spare piece of cloth to check the size and colour are correct, and only then print the full batch of shirts.
sla_notes_daily_life: Businesses producing branded kitenge for weddings, printed packaging for local products, and school event T-shirts all commission patterns printed for these kinds of specific purposes.
sla_exercise: Why is it important to identify the purpose and audience before designing a printed pattern?::So the theme, colours and scale of the pattern suit the intended use, such as a specific event or product.||What should be done before printing the full run of a pattern?::A test print should be made on a sample material to check colour, scale and registration.||Give one example of a specific purpose for which a printed pattern might be designed.::Fabric for a wedding (or a school uniform, or product packaging).

specific_competence_name: Create artistic works using various techniques
sla_assessment_criteria: Detailed 3- dimensional abstract sculptures are well created.
sla_teaching_aids: Chisels|Carving knives mallets|Over-coat|Various species of wood|Soapstone|Clay|Plaster|Papier mache metals|Mallets|Various size of sand-papers|Vanish
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Abstract sculpture represents ideas, emotions or forms without depicting a realistic, recognisable subject, focusing instead on shape, texture and space.
sla_notes_details: Creating a detailed 3-dimensional abstract sculpture involves first deciding on the concept or feeling to be expressed (rather than a specific object to be copied), selecting suitable material (wood, soapstone, clay, plaster, papier mache or metal) and identifying appropriate tools and techniques for that material, then shaping the material through carving, moulding or assembling to develop interesting forms, textures and negative space (the empty areas around and within the sculpture), and refining the surface with sanding and a protective finish. Unlike realistic sculpture, success is judged by how well the form communicates an idea or mood rather than by accuracy to a real subject.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student creating an abstract sculpture representing 'struggle' might twist and layer clay or wood into rough, jagged, interlocking forms rather than carving a recognisable human figure, using texture and shape alone to express the idea.
sla_notes_daily_life: Abstract sculptures used as public monuments, corporate logos in physical form, and modern home decor pieces all apply the same principles of using shape and texture to express an idea rather than to copy reality.
sla_exercise: How does abstract sculpture differ from realistic sculpture?::Abstract sculpture expresses an idea, emotion or form without depicting a recognisable real subject, while realistic sculpture aims to accurately represent one.||Name one material that can be used to create a 3-dimensional abstract sculpture.::Wood, soapstone, clay, plaster, papier mache or metal (any one).||How is the success of an abstract sculpture usually judged?::By how well its form and texture communicate an idea or mood, rather than by its accuracy to a real subject.

specific_competence_name: Create real and abstract drawings and paintings
sla_assessment_criteria: Various sketches from imagination are well created.
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Sketching from imagination requires an artist to visualise and draw a subject, scene or character that does not exist in front of them, relying on memory, creativity and understanding of form.
sla_notes_details: Creating sketches from imagination involves first forming a clear mental image or concept of the subject, drawing on remembered knowledge of proportion, anatomy and perspective built up through earlier observation practice, and using loose exploratory lines to try different possibilities before committing to a final composition. Because there is no real subject to check against, the artist relies on strong foundational skills from observational drawing to keep imagined forms believable and well-proportioned.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student sketching an imagined character for a story, such as a warrior from an invented kingdom, must apply knowledge of human proportion and clothing folds learned from earlier observation exercises, even though no real warrior is in front of them.
sla_notes_daily_life: Book and comic illustrators, game character designers and advertising artists all rely heavily on sketching from imagination to create original characters and scenes that do not exist in reality.
sla_exercise: What is sketching from imagination?::Drawing a subject, scene or character that does not exist in front of the artist, relying on memory and creativity.||Why is earlier observational drawing practice important for sketching from imagination?::It builds knowledge of proportion and form that keeps imagined subjects believable and well-proportioned.||Name one profession that relies heavily on sketching from imagination.::A comic or book illustrator (or a game character designer, or advertising artist).

sla_name: Composing sceneries from imagination by drawing and painting methods
sla_assessment_criteria: Sceneries from imagination using drawing and painting methods are well composed.
sla_teaching_aids: Manila paper|Canvas|Pencils|Paints (water colours|Acrylic|Oil colours) painting brushes|Palette|Linseed oil|Water containers
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Composing an imagined scenery combines creative invention with the technical principles of composition, perspective and colour learned from observational landscape work.
sla_notes_details: Composing a scenery from imagination involves conceiving an invented setting (such as a fantasy village or a future city), applying the same principles of composition, linear and aerial perspective, and depth used in observational scenery painting even though the scene is imagined rather than copied from life, and using colour and light choices deliberately to establish mood, such as warm colours for a lively scene or cool colours for a calm or mysterious one. Consistency of light source and perspective throughout the imagined scene keeps it visually believable despite being invented.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student painting an imagined scenery of a village on a distant hill at sunset would apply the same aerial perspective, lighter and hazier hills fading into the background, that was practised in observational landscape work, while choosing warm orange and pink tones to create a peaceful evening mood.
sla_notes_daily_life: Book cover illustrations, film concept art and mural paintings of imagined scenes in Tanzanian communities all apply this same combination of invented content with real compositional and perspective principles.
sla_exercise: What compositional principles from observational scenery work are still applied when composing an imagined scenery?::Perspective (linear and aerial) and depth, to keep the invented scene visually believable.||How can colour be used to establish mood in an imagined scenery?::Warm colours can create a lively mood while cool colours can create a calm or mysterious mood.||Why must the light source and perspective remain consistent throughout an imagined scenery?::To keep the invented scene visually believable, even though it does not depict a real place.

sla_notes_intro: The Form VI portfolio builds on the Form V portfolio skill but requires a more advanced, professional collection that demonstrates readiness for further study or a career in Fine Art.
sla_notes_details: Preparing an advanced Fine Art portfolio involves selecting the strongest and most technically advanced works across drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture and digital or animated media created during the year, arranging them to show a clear progression of skill and a personal artistic style, writing brief artist statements or captions that explain the concept behind each piece, and presenting the collection professionally, whether as a physical folder, mounted board display or digital file, suitable for assessment or for showing to a college or potential employer. Consistency in presentation quality across all included works is essential.
sla_notes_illustrations: A Form VI student preparing a final portfolio might include one detailed abstract sculpture, one advanced digital animation, and one composed imaginative painting, each with a short written statement explaining its concept, arranged to show growing technical skill from earlier to more recent work.
sla_notes_daily_life: Aspiring artists applying to art colleges or seeking design jobs in Tanzania are typically required to submit exactly this kind of professional portfolio, making this competence directly useful beyond school assessment.
sla_exercise: What distinguishes the Form VI portfolio from the earlier Form V portfolio?::It requires a more advanced, professional collection showing a clear progression of skill and personal style, often across more varied media.||What should accompany each piece in an advanced portfolio besides the artwork itself?::A brief artist statement or caption explaining the concept behind the piece.||Give one real-world use of a well-prepared Fine Art portfolio beyond school assessment.::Applying to an art college or showing work to a potential employer or client.
